He fathers Orion with Euryale, Bellerophon with Eurynome, Neleus and Pelias with Tyro, and is named father of Periclymenus, Butes, Minyas, the Aloiadae, and the twin sons of Actor and Molione. He gives Pegasus to Bellerophon through his father, helps Apollo raise a city wall, and is linked to Orion’s close by Peloris. The account ends by invoking the dark-haired lord’s kindness to sailors.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Heracles is a man on earth and the mightiest of men, born in Thebes as the son of Zeus and Alcmena, also called the son of Amphitryon and the great-hearted offspring of Alcaeus. He is twin brother to Iphiclus, though they differ in parentage and spirit. Described as mighty, valiant, bold-hearted, lion-hearted, most toilful, and most excellent, he is marked by extraordinary strength, violence, hardship, and eventual divine status. He undertakes many deeds and wanderings over land and sea at Eurystheus’s bidding, equipped with a lion-skin, long spear, and great shield, including a shield made by Hephaestus. He travels with Iolaus, serves as his charioteer in the war against Cycnus, kills Cycnus, and then fights and wounds Ares. He defeats Centaurs, releases Prometheus by killing the eagle that consumes his liver, attacks and sacks Pylos after Neleus refuses to purify him for killing Iphitus, and sacks Oechalia for Iole. He also travels across the sea by cauldron, is left behind in Magnesia near Aphetae, repeatedly visits Ceyx’s house at Trachis, and is entertained by Telamon while praying in his lion-skin. He is associated with Black-bottom. After completing grievous labours, he becomes immortal and unageing among the gods. He lives happily in snowy Olympus, where he marries Hebe. He is also said to have loved Deianeira, with whom he had Hyllus, Glenus, Ctesippus, and Odites, and he is identified as Hyllus’s father.

l: Atalanta, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Atalanta, Schoeneus’s beautiful, swift-footed maiden daughter, rejects marriage but races Hippomenes for it; he wins and escapes death by using three golden apples supplied through Aphrodite.

l: Peleus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Peleus, son of Aeacus, is a mortal man honoured by Zeus. After Acastus tries to have him killed by Centaurs, he reaches Phthia with possessions from Iolcus. He marries Thetis with divine approval; after several children perish, he saves Achilles from her cauldron.

l: Thetis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Thetis, daughter of Nereus and mother of Achilles by Peleus, avoids marriage with Zeus to please Hera, after which Zeus decrees she must mate with a mortal. Her divinely honored marriage to Peleus produces children whom she tests in a cauldron, until Peleus saves Achilles. She tells Achilles about Memnon; after his death, she laments with the Muses and her sisters, then carries his body from the pyre to White Island.

l: Phineus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Phineus, son of Phoenix and Cassiopea in Hesiodic traditions, tells Phrixus the way and is blinded, either for this or for choosing long life over sight; father of Thynus and Mariandynus, he is brought by Harpies to milk-feeders.

l: Harpies, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Harpies pursue or flee Zetes and his companions across many lands, tormenting and transporting Phineus; one falls into the Tigris, another reaches the Echinades, and Hesiod says they survive.

l: Shield of Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Shield of Heracles is a vast, glittering, invulnerable shield, its first 53 lines belonging to the Catalogues of Women. Made with enamel, ivory, electrum, gold, cyanus, and adamant, it is chiefly a richly ornamented work modeled on Homer’s description of Achilles’ shield. Its images unfold from Fear at the centre through Strife, battle, Ares, Perseus, monsters, warriors, animals, gods, and a seven-gated city of war and celebration, to contests with a golden tripod and Ocean, swans, and fish enclosing the rim.

l: Cycnus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Cycnus is a gallant, blameless son of Ares, also called son of Poseidon, married to Themistinoe and owner of fine bronze armour. He despoils rich offerings brought to Pytho. Near Apollo’s grove, he confronts Heracles and Iolaus to kill and strip them, refuses warning, attacks, and is killed by Heracles; his armour is stripped.

l: Ceyx, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Ceyx, glorious king of Trachis and friend of the blessed gods, is horse-driving; Heracles visits his feast-holding house there.

l: Eoiae, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_appended_to Catalogues of Women [as a supplementary work] The Eoiae was appended to the Catalogues of Women and consisted of heroines introduced by a recurring formula meaning “Or such as was.” A large fragment survives at the beginning of the Shield of Heracles, and the text suggests that some independent poems may have been expanded from episodes originally belonging to the Eoiae.

l: Aegimius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aegimius is a poem, possibly attributed to Hesiod or Cercops of Miletus. It recounts Phrixus’s reception and purification of the fleece, Thetis testing her children’s mortality in a cauldron, a speaker’s refreshment place, and three Hellenic tribes settling in Crete.

l: Calchas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Calchas is a famous seer who foretells the serpent and sparrows omen. Returning from Troy with Amphilochus, he reaches the place near Clarus on foot, is surpassed by Mopsus in determining figs on a wild fig-tree, and dies of vexation.

l: Teiresias, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Teiresias, a famous seer, lives through seven generations from Cadmus to Eteocles and Polyneices, though some say nine, by Zeus’s ordinance. After seeing mating snakes on Cithaeron, killing the female changes him into a woman; killing the male restores him. His judgment about sexual pleasure brings Hera’s blindness and Zeus’s prophetic power.

l: Proclus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: comments_on verse 828 of Works and Days Proclus discusses The Divination by Birds in relation to verse 828 of Works and Days.

l: Iron Age, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Iron Age is the fifth and present generation of men, marked by unending labor, sorrow, wrongdoing, violence, conflict, and dishonor, ending when Zeus destroys it after corruption becomes complete.

l: Pleiades, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Pleiades are stars, the daughters of Atlas, also called Peleiades in The Astronomy though mortals call them Pleiades. Their movements govern agricultural timing: rising begins harvest, setting marks ploughing, reappearance after forty nights and days signals sharpening the sickle, and their climb ends vineyard digging. They are stormy, disappear or hide, and plunge into the misty sea to escape Orion’s strength.

l: Atlas, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Atlas begets seven daughters called Pleiades, Teygata, Electra, Alcyone, Asterope, Celaeno, Maia, and Merope, and Zeus assigns him to uphold wide Heaven with head and unwearied arms at earth’s borders.

l: Tartarus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Tartarus is an awful primordial place, a great dank gulf deep within Earth. It came into existence near the beginning alongside Chaos, Earth, and Eros. Sealed by shining bronze gates, walls, gloom, and a vast gulf, it imprisons the defeated Titans under warders serving Zeus; later Zeus casts defeated Typhoeus there amid unending clamour and strife.

l: Homeric tradition, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Homeric tradition shaped the style and methods of the Ionic poets. It also led those poets to choose legends beyond the range of the Iliad and Odyssey.

l: Iliad, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Iliad is an epic poem by Homer, central to the Trojan story; it follows the Cypria, occupies its own action, and is followed by the Aethiopis.

l: Odyssey, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: has_author Homer The Odyssey supplied the later central portion of the Trojan narrative, but left untold events concerning Ithaca and the ultimate fate of Odysseus. The Returns brought the general story up to the beginning of the Odyssey, and the Telegony continued it afterward.

l: Trojan story, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_covered_by epic poetry [as a body built up by various Ionic writers] Various Ionic poets gradually built up a body of epic poetry covering the whole Trojan story. The story was expanded backward through the Cyprian Lays and forward through several poems ending with the death of Odysseus.

l: Thebes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Thebes is a city of lovely dances, a seven-gated city whose walls are associated with the Earth-Shaker’s protection. Amphitryon and Alcmena live there and their twin sons are born there. Adrastus flees from it; battle with the Argives brings deaths and last rites for seven. The Theban Cycle treats Oedipus, Polyneices’ expedition, and the Epigoni’s later sack.

l: Titanomachy, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Titanomachy, ascribed to Eumelus of Corinth and Arctinus of Miletus, begins with Theogony and recounts a ten-year, initially balanced war between the Titans and Cronos's gods, ending when Zeus, Cottus, Gyes, and Briareos defeat the Titans.

l: Eumelus of Corinth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Eumelus of Corinth is identified as a possible author of the War of the Titans. He says that Aegaeon was the son of Earth and Sea and an ally of the Titans, and he introduces Zeus dancing; the fragments also attribute to him a description of fish on a shield.

l: Arctinus of Miletus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Arctinus of Miletus was an author credited with the Aethiopis and the Sack of Ilium. Said to have flourished in the first Olympiad, he continued the Trojan story after the Iliad through deaths of Penthesilea, Memnon, and Achilles, ending with Ilium’s fall and aftermath.

l: Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Oedipus, central figure of the Story of Oedipus, is father of sons born to Euryganeia. He owns a silver table and golden cup from his father’s treasures. Distressed when Polyneices presents treasures of Cadmus and angered by a haunch sent by his sons, he curses them and prays to Zeus and the deathless gods that they kill one another and go to Hades.

l: Polyneices, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Polyneices, Oedipus’s heaven-born, golden-haired son, serves wine at Cadmus’s table; the treasures bring Oedipus misery, curses his sons, and precedes Polyneices’s fatal quarrel with Eteocles.

l: Adrastus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Adrastus flees Thebes in miserable garments with the black-maned Areion, then laments his dead host after the seven receive last rites, praising him as seer and spearman.

l: Trojan Cycle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Trojan Cycle is a set of component epics that, with the Homeric poems, connects events before and after the Iliad and Odyssey. It unfolds through Cyprian Lays, Aethiopis, Little Iliad, Sack of Troy, Returns, and Telegony; evidence survives chiefly as fragments and Proclus’s abridgment preserved by Photius.

l: Cyprian Lays, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Cyprian Lays, attributed to Stasinus of Cyprus or Hegesinus of Salamis, precede the Iliad, tracing Zeus’s purpose, the apple of discord, Helen’s rape, and the Trojan War’s opening through Achilles and Agamemnon’s quarrel.

l: The Aethiopis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Aethiopis is a five-book work attributed to Arctinus of Miletus that follows the Iliad and narrates events after Hector’s death. It unfolds through the arrivals and deaths of Penthesilea and Memnon, the death of Antilochus, Achilles’ death and burial, and the dispute between Odysseus and Aias over Achilles’ arms.

l: The Little Iliad, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Little Iliad is a four-book epic poem ascribed to Lesches of Pyrrha or Mitylene, though another record calls it Homer’s composition. It elaborates material associated with the Sack of Troy: Achilles’ arms are adjudged to Odysseus, Aias becomes mad, Philoctetes and Neoptolemus arrive, the wooden horse is made, the Palladium is stolen, and the sack unfolds.

l: The Sack of Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Sack of Ilium is a two-book epic poem by Arctinus of Miletus. It describes the wooden horse, Laocoon, Sinon, the Greeks’ return from Tenedos, the capture, sack, and burning of Ilium, division of the spoils, and the Greeks’ departure; it precedes The Returns.

l: Returns, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Returns is a five-book epic poem attributed to Agias or Hegias of Troezen. Following the Sack of Ilium and preceding the Odyssey, it recounts Greek heroes’ disputed, storm-hit journeys home: the quarrel of Agamemnon and Menelaus, Neoptolemus’s overland route, Agamemnon’s murder, and Orestes and Pylades’ vengeance. It ends with Menelaus’s return, while also including Hades, Medea, Antiope, and Tantalus.

l: The Telegony, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Telegony is a two-book poem by Eugammon of Cyrene, following the Odyssey in the epic sequence. It continues Odysseus’s story through adventures in Thesprotis and his return to Ithaca, ending with his death at Telegonus’s hands, Circe’s grant of immortality, and marriages among surviving characters.

l: Lesches of Pyrrha or Mitylene, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a poet Lesches of Mitylene is identified as the author of the four-book Little Iliad. The fragments also attribute to him accounts of the quarrel between Aias and Odysseus, Odysseus’s disguise, and details of the fall of Ilium.

l: Paris, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Paris kills Achilles together with Apollo.
